prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle

statement.case_for: I keep B019 as my preferred configuration after the full first-round exchange. The test I apply is that the prize goes to the original, experimentally verified discovery, and that we can be sure who did it. For B019 the chain is short and documentable: the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald calculation said where the flat bands would appear, and the 2018 experiments from the Jarillo-Herrero group found correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle, in a system made of carbon that nobody had expected to behave this way. Independent groups using transport, scanning probes and spectroscopy have since reproduced the phases, and the platform has spread to twisted TMDs and fractional Chern insulators, so the observation is robust and not a single-laboratory result. The citation I propose is narrow on purpose. It rewards the prediction of the bands and the observation of the phases, and says nothing about the pairing mechanism or the nature of individual correlated states. That separates what has been verified from what is still argued, which is how I would answer Johansson and Danielsson on maturity. I have not moved to B042 because I did not hear a new fact in round 1 that makes me confident the lattice-clock credit is original in the sense I require for both names, but I regard B042 as a fully defensible prize and I can vote for it without reservation if the committee prefers it.
statement.case_against: The strongest objections are the ones I raised in round 1 and that colleagues have sharpened. First, maturity: eight years is short, the pairing mechanism is open, and sample and twist-angle disorder still complicate the picture, so a prize now rests on a phenomenology and not on a settled explanation. Second, attribution: under a three-person limit Yuan Cao, first author of the two 2018 papers and the student who did the decisive measurements, cannot be named, and Dean, Kim, Young, Efetov, Ashoori and others have claims on parts of the field, as does the earlier twist-angle theory of Lopes dos Santos and collaborators. I read the history as clean at the level of group leadership but not at the level of who actually made the measurement, and the committee record should say so openly. If, on reading the 2011 and 2018 records again, the committee finds the theory priority or the experimental priority genuinely contested, then B042, with two names that every proposer agreed on, is the safer prize, and the case against waiting is weaker than the case against crediting the wrong people.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock has a quantitatively verified result today, that the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation are separable from the 2005 comb prize, and asks whether the committee gains anything by waiting on twisted bilayers while the clock case is complete.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument for B042 and I take it seriously. You are right that the committee does not gain by waiting if the discovery is already settled, and my answer on B019 is that the discovery of the phases is settled while their explanation is not, so the citation does not have to wait. On the clocks, you have convinced me that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct conceptual step and not an extension of the comb, and that the 2005 and 2012 overlap is not disqualifying. My remaining question from round 1 is still open: Katori's proposal and first demonstration are original, but I would need the expert evidence to say what Ye's clocks added that was first and not only better. If the evidence says the 1e-18 regime and its systematics were opened by the JILA work, then I would be satisfied.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B032, argues that the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux is established and that source identification at 3-4 sigma is a qualification rather than a reason to wait, and says the 2002 prize is not an obstacle.
responses.response: I agree with you that the committee has honoured discoveries before the full interpretation was in, and that is exactly the logic I apply to B019. That consistency matters to me, and it is why I do not accept the open pairing mechanism as a reason to wait. Where I still differ is on B032 itself. In experimental physics I would want to be absolutely sure of the original-work attribution, and the IceCube credit chain is the problem: AMANDA, Baikal, DUMAND and ANTARES were each in some sense first, the discovery paper is by a collaboration of hundreds, and two names cannot capture who did the original experiment. I would support B032 only if the expert reports show that Halzen and Spiering are the decisive pair, and I would not put it ahead of a candidate whose credit is already documented.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B042 and says the open superconducting pairing mechanism in twisted bilayers favours waiting a few years, while the clock case is robust across laboratories and has a clean two-name attribution.
responses.response: I agree that robustness across laboratories is the right standard, and B042 meets it. I disagree that an open mechanism is a reason to wait, because the committee has not required that for earlier prizes in condensed matter, and what has been reproduced independently is the observation of the phases, not a theory of them. If the citation names only the flat-band prediction and the observed states, the open mechanism does not touch it. I would accept your point if the reproducibility of the superconductivity itself were in doubt, but in my reading the community has confirmed it across many devices and groups, even if sample dependence is real.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B019 but names B042 as the better-settled discovery if the field is judged too young, and raises a two-part prize pairing B019 with a more mature candidate as an open question.
responses.response: We hold the same position, so I will say where I would not follow you. I would not recommend a two-part prize. Pairing B019 with a more mature candidate would dilute the single clear statement a physics prize should make, and it would force us to choose a partner whose credit is itself contested. On the choice between B019 and B042 I agree with you that B042 is the cleaner fall-back, and I would say so explicitly to the committee: if the vote does not favour B019, I will support B042 and not B028 or any of the AMO alternatives.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B042 and said that the omission of Krivanek and Dellby makes the B028 allocation hard to defend, and that he is willing to reconsider B028 only if the TEM and STEM correction lines can be separated fairly.
responses.response: Thank you for that, and I agree that the gap is real. It is also why I have moved away from B028 and do not put it among my alternatives this time. I should also be plain that this is my own field, and I do not think I can be the member who decides whether the TEM and STEM correction lines can be split, so I would not ask the committee to rely on my judgment there. I note that the same test, whether we can identify the people who did the original work, is the one I apply to B019, and I accept that it is imperfect there too, which is why I regard B042 as the cleaner outcome if the credit review for B019 does not hold.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, on rereading the 2011 and 2018 records, finds the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero experiment to be the decisive pair, given the earlier twist-angle theory of Lopes dos Santos and collaborators and the omitted first author Yuan Cao.

Whether the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated states could change in the next few years in a way that makes the narrow citation look premature; I judge this unlikely for the phases themselves but cannot be sure.

Whether Ye's record-setting lattice clocks contain original steps that Katori's group did not take first, and whether anyone beyond Katori and Ye has a priority claim; I cannot settle this without the expert reports.
Whether the committee would treat a lattice-clock prize as a discovery in physics and not as a refined instrument, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My own field is transmission electron microscopy, and B028 (aberration-corrected electron microscopy) falls directly in it; I know the aberration-correction community, have no direct tie to Rose, Urban or Haider, and I have moved away from that ballot and will not advocate it. I have no apparent connection to any credited name on B019, B042 or B058. Johansson is a colleague at Chalmers, and I have been aware of his recusal flags on B049, B051 and B038. Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, but he has no stake in B019 or B042.
